THE SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION

Oral History
Interview with Marshall Royal by Patricia Willard
Reel 1
October 25, 1977

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
PROCEEDINGS
clh
This is October 25th, 1977, and this is the oral history (Inaudible) with Marshal Royal. Marshal, let's first get your birthdate confirmed. Is it December 5th, 1912, as has been printed?
Correct, correct.
And you were born in Sapulpa, Oklahoma?
Correct.
Had your family lived in Oklahoma --
No.
How did you happen to be born in Sapulpa?
Coming on the way to California from Texas.
Was Texas the family home?

My mother was born in Denison, Texas. My father was born in Sherman, Texas. My father was the leader of a orchestra. As a matter of fact, he was the leader of the first jazz band that ever came out of North Texas. It was the Marshal Royal Band. He played in the World's Fair in St. Louis, I believe, somewhere around 1892 or somewhere around that era and he was also in San Francisco during the big earthquake with his band. He was one of the first guys that had a band of that type that was considered as being a reading band.
In the old days, Scott Joplin used to bring many of

his scores down to let my father's orchestra try them out for him and try to put them together because my dad was a music teacher and my uncle was in his band, was also a music teacher and a very accomplished musician.

My mother was a piano teacher and she was quite accomplished. So they could read anything that Scott Joplin wrote and do it in this way. My mother used to play all of the Maple Leaf Rags and things of Scott.

So, in having their band, they came together, the two brothers, Marshal and Ernest Royal, and my mother was Ernestine Royal, the pianist. They were coming from Texas, going to the Land of the Free, and California, when I say "Land of the Free," was, my father told me, as long as I lived, never go down South again, because opportunities weren't available there for an intelligent young man and that's what he wanted me to be and so, that's the reason we were on our way to California.

So, on the way to California, they stopped with the band to play a couple of dates and during the playing of these dates, my father sort of liked the location around that particular area and saw that it was conducive to entertainment work. So, he stopped over in Sapulpa and sent for his mother and bought her a house there and then he was a pretty good man with his hands, he built a house for my mother and he and I was born in that house about a year or so later.

So we stayed there for about -- in Sapulpa for about four years and then he finally decided that it was time that he took me to the so-called "Land of the Free," where I could get a decent education and be a man. So we came to California in 1918, in the spring of 1918, right before -- the World War I was still going on then. I got into California just in time to catch the flu and almost died, was delirious for two, three or four weeks with the flu, which nobody knew anything about at that time because it was the first epidemic of that type that was ever known in the United States.
Incidentally, my doctor at that time was a fellow by the name of Gordon. He was Dexter Gordon's father, which leads into another story that I could probably tell on.
(Inaudible). Well, you can tell it now if you want.

And he -- this doctor was a lover of music. So he took a very good liking to my father and my mother and he gave special care to me and he would, even though he was overburdened with patients during this time of the big epidemic -- it was almost a plague -- in 1918, he made sure that he got by my house once or twice everyday to make special care that I was able to get along with it and get over with it.

So, after many years, he bore a son by the name of Dexter Gordon and I was -- before he died, the father of Dexter Gordon, he promised me that if ever there was a time that I could do anything to help his son, to do so. I had a chance to

repay him for his kindnesses when Lionel Hampton first started his band in 1940. In the fall of 1940, we had an empty spot in the saxophone section and his son Dexter was coming up, was a young teenager -- he was about 15, 16 years old -- and he wanted to play. So I got a chance to repay his dad for all of his kindness by getting Dexter on the Lionel Hampton Band, which was the first band that Dexter Gordon ever worked with. He went right on from there. I sort of looked after him, sort of like a father, for a while, until he got his feet on the ground.
So, that's that story.
What was Dr. Gordon's first name? Do you remember?
Can't think right off, right now.
Your father's name then was also Marshal Royal?
Right.
And his brother was Ernest Royal?
That's right.
So there were a pair of brothers named Marshal and Ernest Royal before.
That's right. So it was Marshal Senior and Marshal Junior, and then my kid brother was named after his brother. So we had the same thing going on a couple generations apart.
What can you tell me about your father's band? How big was it?

Well, I'll tell you, in those days, when he first started out with his band, he used to travel. He used to carry about six pieces in his band but they all doubled on different instruments. The saxophone players, they all played violin. They played mandolins. They played guitars. They played baritone horns and trumpets. They all doubled.
It was the sort of a thing where anything that was needed to be played could be played by them and if it came a chance to have a bigger band, well, they added according to what they wanted.

As a matter of fact, at one time, they had a barn-storming band that used to go around and play and if they'd get into a town, they would have a baseball team among their band and they would play whoever was in that town that could play them. One time, they had a chance to play against Rogers Hornsby (PHONETIC) down in that area, who was a -- turned out to be one of the greatest baseball players of all time in the Hall of Fame.

It was quite an experience with them because they couldn't compete at all with these guys that really knew how to play ball and I think the only time they were able to get up to bat, I think Rogers Hornsby and his group had to put themselves out. They just allowed them to get up to bat. So,
it was a territorial band, but it was a good one and my father was instrumental in teaching many, many of the young people that weren't able to have lessons in that area and that era.

As a matter of fact, he gained his knowledge by accepting a job in a girls' college as a waiter and a cook, so that after the schooltime hours were out, where he served and cooked the meals, he could go to the professor of music in that particular academy and get himself a true education, which he did for a couple of years after hours, after his work was done.
What was the name of that school?
It was called Kitkey (PHONETIC) College. I think it was in Texas.
Do you know how to spell that?

K-i-t -- was the first name, and in Key, I think, was k-e-y. Because I've never seen it actually spelled. I just heard him speaking of it, speaking of Kitkey. But it was a girls' school actually, but there were some very fine professors there that knew what it was all about. So, that's how he happened to get his --
How old was he then?
Oh, he was a young man. He was like 16, 18 years of age, and so that's how he happened to get his education.
How many instruments did he play?
Well, he could just about play anything that there was to be played, but he specialized in the reeds and he was, in that time, a very good mandolin and banjo player.
Would you know the names of anybody who worked in that band?

I don't think there would be actually anyone that ever actually came out of there to be in the professional world. Of course, that would -- my father, at this time, would be like 97 or 98 years old, so this was an entirely different era that we're speaking of. He used to play the big shows that used to come through like Drake and Walker (PHONETIC) and things of that type, which were -- and the Whitman Sisters shows, that were practically the better line, black shows of that era.
You say they'd come through. You mean, come through where you were living in Texas?

They would come through the different parts of Texas on tour and he would travel with them and go to Galveston or -- which was a big town in those days, you know. There was a whole lot happening in Galveston in those days. And went to St. Louis and Kansas City and went up also, well, into Canada, traveling with those shows in those days.
When you say he had a territory band, it was extra-large piece of territory.
Yeah, well, he --
-- to go through Canada and --

Well, really, speaking of territorial, I was speaking in the lines of the North Texas group and into Oklahoma, then they would also go into Hot Springs, Arkansas, into the spas down there, where the multi-millionaires used to come in those days.
How did he happen to be working as far West as San Francisco?

Well, he just went on a tour, went through Canada and went on across from the eastern part of Canada on over to the western part and came down the West Coast. When he came down, he got to San Francisco, just in time to be in the big earthquake.
And did your mother travel with him frequently?

My mother wasn't with him at that time. That was before her time. He was a bit older than my mother. So, she only started traveling after he came down and resettled again in the area around North Texas, in that area, and that's when he married her.
What was your mother's name?

Ernestine Walton. Her father was one of the first educators in North Texas. He was in the group with Douglass and the other big-time Negro educators of that time. He happened to be in the part of -- he came down from the North. He

had -- his people were actually descendants from the Canadian side and they came down into North Texas and settled in Denison, Texas. He raised, on top of being a schoolteacher and the head of the school there, that was in his name, the Walton School in Denison, Texas, he was also a raiser of race horses that he bred and sold and took down to race around Hot Springs, Arkansas and those types of places down there.
So how did your mother happen to get interested in music? Were there any other music in your family?

Well, she was -- she just happened to take music. Her mother had the good fortune of going to college as a girl and she learned some music, so when she married my grandfather, well, she sort of tried to pass a few things on to her children and she passed the music thing on to my mother. So, she ended up in that particular grouping around that town. Always you have to have somebody that plays the piano in the church and plays the organ, things like that. So, that's what happened with my mother.
And had your mother ever played any jazz or did that happen (inaudible)? When she met your father? Or rags or...

In those days, jazz was a word that was very vague. It was ragtime in those days. She could play -- ragtime music was usually music that was written and not played extemporaneously as jazz is, off the top of your skull. So,
since she was a learned person on the piano, all she had to do was have the music passed out to her and she started playing it. So, she turned out to be a very excellent ragtime piano player.
So she joined your father's band when they got married?
That's right.
And then they traveled together (inaudible)? from that point on.

That's it. I slept behind the piano from the time I was two or three months old on my father's overcoat. Anytime they would go out of town or across town or anywhere else to keep her in the band, I was the baby back in behind the piano on the overcoats.
How old were you, your earliest memories of being there during the band's performances?

I don't know. It's rather hard to really tack yourself down, but there have been studies of children that have grown up and people have tried to pin down the earliest age that a person is actually able to recollect, but I can remember -- and it was told to me by my parents -- that I hummed tunes in their entirety before I was able to talk. So, -- which I believe is true, because as I came into the music business, I discovered that I had -- I don't know whether they call it 'perfect pitch' or 'absolute pitch' or whatever it happens to

be. But I had what they call "pitch" and I could tell the pitch of any note, whether it was the squeaking of a brake on a streetcar or the tooting of a whistle on a train, I could tell exactly what pitch that was, from the time that I can remember being a person.
Well, you may have had some prenatal influence, too.
I don't know.
You probably got those (Inaudible) vibrations from the music. (inaudible).
Maybe those things happen, so it's quite possible.
So you were on the road with the band from the beginning?

Yep. Yeah, I was there from my beginning. So, I'm a music man. That's all I know. And as a matter of fact, it's all I really wanted to know, was as a vocation, was music. I keep up-to-date on all other things of world happenings. It's a practice of mine to awaken at daybreak and get the paper and I read the paper from the first page all through the financial page every morning before I finish my coffee. But so far as ever being -- wanting to be anything other than a musician, nothing else ever passed my mind.
You just sort of knew you would be.
I had to be. There was no way I could

miss it. It wasn't forced on me at all. My father never forced anything on me. My mother never forced anything on me. They had an idea that they would have liked for me to have complete knowledge of the piano, which I positively refused to play, because I had the complex all built in my mind that a piano was only supposed to be played by a woman because my mother was a woman and she played the piano and I would be less than a man if I played the piano. I positively refused to play the piano.

But yet, I played the violin, which in the eyes of many, was considered as a sissy instrument. But my father was intelligent enough from the time that I got into junior high school playing the violin to also give me a set of boxing gloves, so that -- and sent me down to the gym to learn how to take care of myself, because he knew somebody was going to be picking at me because I was playing the violin.
So, I learned how to be a pretty good boxer by being a violin player.
That's great. You started playing -- your first instrument was violin?
Violin, yes.
You were how old?
I was actually about five years old when I had my -- when I really got into actually playing and studying hard on the violin, when I was about five. My father bought me

a half-size violin because I was much too small to play even a three-quarter size violin, so I had a little half-size one. And I played it and I learned how to play chords on it and -- which also taught me to automatically become a banjo player, because I learnt the fingerings of the chords and it was just a matter of picking up the banjo and finding out the different distance between the notes as in comparison with my half-size violin. So, I was an automatic, built-in banjo player.
You say you were five years old before you did any serious studying.
Yeah.
What did you do before five?

Well, I tinkered around with whatever was around the house. I used to get the mandolins and play with them, the round-backed, beautiful, inlaid mandolins and I would tinker around and just try to play anything that I could put my hands on. But then, my dad gave me this violin and then I had to study everyday, from the time I was five years old.
What kind of music were you playing? What were you studying?

I studied legitimate music. Just a legitimate background. By the time I got to junior high school, I was the concert master in the band. I was always the concert master in every orchestra that I ever played. I played with the Junior Philharmonic Orchestra here as a child in Los Angeles. I

think the conductor there was Rothstein, Rosenthal, Rothstein or something. I can't think of that man's name. He was the conductor of the Los Angeles Philharmonic Orchestra. So I played there with the Junior Philharmonic Orchestra when I was in junior high school and in high school, legitimate music.
At what age did you take a second instrument?

Well, when I graduated from junior high school in June the 27th, 1927, when I walked down the aisle, I was the last one in the class that walked down because alphabetically, there was nobody in the class with -- that came in my line after the R's, so I was the last one in my class to walk across the stage and out of the auditorium and when I got there, my uncle had a little box waiting for me and I asked him what it was and he says, 'This is your new clarinet.' So, I really didn't know anything about it. It was unexpected and I hadn't really thought much about it. I used to tinker around with some of my dad's clarinets. He had eight or nine of them around the house. But they were what they call the Albert system (PHONETIC) clarinets, which was the old-style clarinets. There's hardly anyone in this world that plays them anymore outside of Barney Bigard and Procope.
My uncle had a brand new Boehm system clarinet waiting there for me. So I said, 'What is this?' He says, 'That's your clarinet.' And he says, 'When you start to high

school in September, you're going to be playing the first clarinet in the band." This was the night of June the 27th, 1927, when I graduated from junior high school. So, I says, "Okay, Uncle." So, that was on a Friday night. The next morning, I turned the corner running around the corner of our house, running to go swimming at the YMCA early in the morning and when I got there and turned the corner, I ran right into my uncle's arms, and he says, "This is it." I says, "What you mean?" He says, "You start your lessons today." I said, "Okay," so I had a lesson everyday, starting from the 28th of June until the fifth of September when I went into senior high school and when I went to senior high school, I was the first clarinet player in the band.
That's great.

So I had a lesson everyday and I couldn't go swimming or to play baseball or anything else, until I had my lesson and had studied at least an hour or hour and a half of what my lesson was, which I would immediately memorize and then I would be able to go in swimming or play baseball during the summer.
Did you enjoy the clarinet then?

Yeah, I liked it very much. The clarinet is a challenging instrument. As a matter of fact, the clarinet today is the bugaboo of most all reed players. They look at it and just cringe when they see a clarinet. They're very, very

proud to try to outlaw it now and play a flute instead, because it gives them quite a working over and they hate them, most of the modern saxophone players. As a matter of fact, nine out of ten of the modern saxophone players are very lousy clarinet players, although most of them are fairly good flute players but they can't play a clarinet.
You don't hear much clarinet now (Inaudible).

No, no, they were very glad to find something else to use as a substitute, which the flute happened to fall quite in line, although that's a wonderful instrument, the flute. But it is no more wonderful than the clarinet itself, when played correctly.
Do you still play the clarinet?
Occasionally, if it's called for.
You don't get much (inaudible), do you?

No, nobody writes for a clarinet. So if you don't write for it, you don't play it. But that was pretty well my favorite instrument. As a matter of fact, when I went to work with the Basie Band in '51, when I went -- that was January, 1951 -- I went to his band primarily as a clarinet player, because I was replacing Buddy De Franco, who was an excellent clarinet player, one of the best jazz clarinet players there ever was. So, in replacing him, Basie was kind enough to remember that I was an exceptional player. So I went in there and I had to be an exceptional player because the company

of the other two horns was extremely perilous. Clark Terry was playing the trumpet and Wardell Grey (PHONETIC) was playing the tenor saxophone and if you couldn't play, you just as well go home with them.
(Laughter.)

So, it was very interesting, because we only had the three horns and it was a workout every night and if you couldn't play clarinet in that band -- if you couldn't play clarinet, period -- you just couldn't hold that job. So, it was a lot of fun.
Tell me about -- I rarely see your name spelled correctly. I know you have told me it was Marshal with one L.

Well, I'll tell you all about that, for what it's worth. My father spelled his name with one L, so being a junior, I should spell mine with one L. But it so happens that in the signing of my birth certificate, the doctor that signed my birth certificate also signed my name in. When he did, he signed it with two L's. I never realized that I had two L's in my name until I sent to Sapulpa, Oklahoma, to get my birth certificate so that I could get a passport and once I found my birth certificate, I found out that this doctor had entered me as having two L's, which legitimately is the correct way for that type of a noun, being a proper noun in the name, it should be spelled with two L's, because the

other marshal is usually associated with the other type of -- like the grand marshal or the marshal of this or the marshal of that, and not as a proper noun, so that's why you see it spelled both ways. I accept it both ways. I'll accept a check with one L or two L's and sometimes, when I go to cash a check -- as a matter of fact, all times when I cash a check -- I always look over it first to see if it's spelled with one L or two L's and sometimes, if I have three or four checks to cash, half of them are spelled with one L and half of them are spelled with two of them and so, that's the way it is. I accept checks in both L's.
Okay. Was your father's name spelled that way for any particular reason? Was (inaudible)? he named after a marshal?
That's the way he spelled his name, and that's it.
And actually, that's the way yours is spelled. It's just that the birth certificate (inaudible). 's incorrect
That's the way --
And reference books.

For me to be a junior, legitimately, I'm supposed to have it spelled the same as my father's name, or else I'm not a junior. So, to keep it that way, I just spell it that way. On top of that, in spelling M-a-r-s-h-a-l, with one L, and R-o-y-a-l, that comes to 12 and I always wanted, when I was a kid, to have a watch with my name on it, so I

finally got to the place where I could save up enough money one time to get me a diamond-faced watch with diamonds with my name spelled all the way around it. So, I had one for each letter of the day -- 1, 2, 3, 4, up until 12 -- and M-a-r-s-h-a-l R-o-y-a-l spells exactly one dozen, 12. So, I kept it that way and I never, as a young man, I never changed it and never used two L's.
Well, we'll get it right on this though both the books... one, even (inaudible).
It doesn't really matter. I answer to both of them. The particular book, this last book that you have, I think it had two L's, doesn't it?
Yeah, the Chilton (PHONETIC) book.
Yeah.
And the Feather Encyclopedia does, too.

Yeah, but it doesn't really matter. I'm the same guy and I've never known another fella in this world to be named Marshal Royal, other than my father. So, there's no denying who I am anywhere in this world.
Maybe we got the identities straight. When you came to California, your first stop was Los Angeles? Was that your destination (inaudible)?
That's right. That was it.
Why did your father pick Los Angeles rather than northern California?

Well, one of the bass -- the bass player in my father's orchestra had moved to California and he had grown rather successful. He was lightly into real estate and he was also a deputy sheriff and in those days way back in the teens, deputy sheriff sort of carried a little weight around around town, strictly because he could afford to have a great big .45 on his hip, walking down. So that demands a little bit of respect, the other side of the track, anyway.

He was a great admirer of my father's. His name was Wood Wilson. He was doing very well in California and used to always write to my dad and tell him, say, "You should come out here because you can make it," because my father had taught him a whole lot about music during the years that he had worked with my dad as a bass player. His brother also worked with my dad's band. He had a twin brother. One of them played the bass and the other played the guitar.
the twin brother's name?
Do you remember (inaudible)?

Yeah, the bass player's name was Wood Wilson and the guitar player was Tuck Wilson, T-u-c-k. They were twin brothers and they were constantly writing my dad, "Come on out, because it's good out here." So, when we came to California, they had the house next to his house all readied for rental purposes and we rented all except one room in the house, which the fellow that owned the house remained in and stayed in and we rented the rest of the house.
We lived there for two or three years next door to this friend of my dad's until we got a little bit bigger house, where we could stretch out a little bit more about a block away.
Where was it you lived first? Do you know? What street?
(Inaudible)?

I lived on 34th Street in Los Angeles. I lived on 33rd Street when we first came to Los Angeles, the 1100 block. Then I moved around the corner to the 1200 block on 34th Street, at 1233. That was it, 1233 East 34th Street.
How long did you live there?

I lived there from about 1921 until 1939 or somewhere around that era. Yes, that's when -- it was 1939. Then at that time, everything was sort of moving a little bit further West, because the street I used to have to cross one-half block from my house was unpaved and when it rained, the mud came up to your knees. It was the same street from which I gained a lot of my knowledge of Jefferson High School, on the East Side of town, and thinking back over those days of struggling through that mud, I feel as though I'm very fortunate to have survived because I really didn't think I'd make it this far.
Why not?
It was just depressing to live so far behind the Iron Curtain and I was in a very, very depressed neighborhood. People were poor. I mean poor. Any time a kid

would come to school with a bean sandwich, he was pretty poor. Although my dad always provided a little bit better because he was fortunate enough to be able to demand a pretty good salary for his one-nighters and things he did. He didn't work these regular dance halls and things in those days. He worked special jobs for the people that were the 'get-rich-quick' Hollywood crowd in the movie industry that was just coming up at that time. He worked parties for Gloria Swanson and the producers like James Cruse (PHONETIC) the director, who was married to Betty Compston (PHONETIC) and those were the type of people that he did weekend parties and things for.

At the time when they were subdividing and putting this new area over here right outside of Pasadena called Flint-ridge and La Crescenta, when they were subdividing, we -- my dad played for subdivisions of all of that. He used to play for the clambakes down at what is now Palos Verdes off the beach, when they were subdividing that, when it was nothing but ground. He played for the subdivisions of those things and he was able to name his own price for jobs and so in doing so, he also had as his clientele Marco Hellman (PHONETIC), who was the president of the Hellman Bank, which in Los Angeles, turned out to be the Bank of America.
He played for the stag parties for Jack Warner and Warner Brothers, things like that. The first time I ever went to a stag party and saw what a real stag party was was the big-

time party they gave at the Beverly Hills Riding Academy for Jack Warner when he was taking his first trip to Europe. I was very, very low teenager. I was -- as a matter of fact, it was in 1926, so you can add from 1926 from 1912 and you'll get it. I was 14 years old. I worked with the family orchestra at this big stag party and the funny thing is nobody actually knew it was a stag party. My dad didn't know it was a stag party because when the call came in, my father took his regular orchestra out there, which was -- included in there was my mother, who was a piano player, and he brought me, and I was just a early teenager. This was a stag party to end all stag parties. Anything that a man is supposed to see in life and was able to have seen it in pornography was there that night.

So, when we got there and Marco Hellman saw my mother, he says, "My God, Royal," he says, "what is she doing here?" He says, "Why didn't you tell me what kind of party it was?" So he says, "She'll have to go home." So my dad says, "Naturally." So, he put her in his Rolls Royce and had her driven home by his chauffeur. But my dad made sure that I stayed because he says, he wanted to make sure that I saw everything that was happening in this life, so that nothing would be new to me.
Got it all at once.
And I got it all at once. Just like my dad would always give me a drink of whiskey from the time I was

a toddler. He'd give me some, if it was nothing but a half a teaspoon full, because he says, he always wanted me to know what liquor was, so that it would never excite me when it was put on me at a later age. And so, for that matter, I only managed to get drunk about twice in my life, strictly accidental. So, that was a good lesson to me, too, because he always wanted me to know exactly what was happening in life first-hand, so I wouldn't have to get it second-hand from anybody else, which is a good idea for these kids running around now that if their fathers and mothers would tell them about what marijuana is and what everything else is, not necessarily to give it to them, just tell them the truth about it, then they won't be all mixed up and upset when somebody lays it on them down the line.

Did your father just get established upon arrival? with all these wealthy people immediately? (Inaudible) Did he get introduced? I mean, he came into town -- he hadn't worked Los Angeles before, had he?

Well, when you come into places like that, well, then you work sometimes with other people as side men and their orchestras and then you get seen and respected and people start liking. So they start calling you. He worked in in that manner by respect and --
So, well, he wasn't here very long before he was --
That's right.
-- leading his own band --
That's right.
-- and working rather steadily.
That's the idea.
And so when you started to play professionally, it was with the band --
I started with the family band, yeah.
And your uncle was still --
Yep.
-- in the band?
That's right.
He came out with your father, right?
That's right. Everybody came together. Father, uncle and mother and I was born down the line on the way.
(Laughter.)
And so it was after you got here that your brother was born.

I would be, too.
Uh-huh.

Japan.
Oh, yes.

The next thing to that is country and western and even that is derived from a lot of the European types of songs and things, where the cowboys sing to their herds the way that the shepherds and things sang to their herds in the old country. (Inaudible).

Sailors in the old days had a certain type of things that they liked and it wasn't high-class jazz. They liked to be nostalgic and have some guy sing "Harbor Lights" to them or, you know, all of those kind of things, to remind them of when they were away on their ship, wondering what their girl was doing back on the seashore, you know? One of the things about jazz music is most all jazz in every form is a black heritage. That can be proven. There's no doubt about it. Usually, new ideas come from jazz guys out of frustration and pride and other things that go toward trying to be inventive. A lot of music as it is is just -- comes from that way, from guys that have been denied and just do something else. Sometime it's almost a matter of fighting
back on the musical society, to play something that another guy can't do.

For years and years, there were probably only two or three or four jazz bands that ever made records and up until the '30s and '40s, there were no black bands that had recording contracts anywhere. So a lot of the things that have come out of jazz are just out of frustration and pure meanness sometimes, to just try to do something that nobody else can do, and black guys have so much pride about themselves that once the other people start finding out and start mimicking them, rather than go back and play what the other guy has learned how to do and is mimicking well, he'll get himself something new to play and go into a different phase, just to screw them all up, so they don't know where they are.
